title: What must employers in Japan do to prevent customer harassment from October 2026?
description: Japan's customer harassment duty from October 1, 2026: Article 33 measures, MHLW Notice No. 51 of 2026, training expectations, and how to evidence them.
shortAnswer: From October 1, 2026, every employer in Japan must take employment management measures against customer harassment under Article 33 of the Act on Comprehensive Promotion of Labor Policies, added by Act No. 63 of 2025. MHLW Notice No. 51 of 2026 requires a policy to respond firmly and protect workers, predefined response procedures, a consultation desk, prompt case handling, a plan for especially malicious conduct, privacy protection, and no retaliation.
keyTakeaways: Customer harassment (kasutamā harasumento) is conduct by customers, business partners, facility users or others connected with the business that exceeds what is socially acceptable given the nature of the work and harms the worker's working environment. All three elements must be met.

The duty applies to all employers regardless of size from October 1, 2026, the date set by Cabinet Order No. 17 of 2026. The MHLW Guideline (Notice No. 51 of 2026) was promulgated on February 26, 2026.

The Guideline sets ten required measures. Three are specific to customer harassment: a policy to respond firmly and protect workers, predefined response procedures made known to workers, and a prepared response to especially malicious conduct.
Training is named throughout the Guideline as an accepted way to meet the measures, and Article 34(2) adds an effort duty to train workers so they do not harass other employers' workers.
There is no criminal penalty. The Minister can give advice, guidance and recommendations under Article 42 and publish the name of an employer that ignores a recommendation.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) and Prefectural Labor Bureaus
appliesTo: All employers in Japan, regardless of size, from October 1, 2026
Host companies that receive dispatched (temporary agency) workers, for those workers
Managers and supervisors, who are named as recipients of the policy and response procedures
Customer facing workers in retail, hospitality, transport, healthcare, care, education, call centers and similar roles
Consultation desk, HR and legal staff who handle customer harassment cases

sections.heading: Which law makes customer harassment prevention mandatory in Japan?

blocks.text: Article 33 of the Act on Comprehensive Promotion of Labor Policies and Stabilization of Employment and Enrichment of Workers' Vocational Lives (労働施策総合推進法, Act No. 132 of 1966) makes customer harassment prevention mandatory. Article 33 was inserted by Act No. 63 of 2025, promulgated on June 11, 2025, and [Cabinet Order No. 17 of 2026](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001662631.pdf) set its commencement date as October 1, 2026. The Japanese text in force is on [e-Gov Laws](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/341AC0000000132/20261001_507AC0000000063).

Article 33(1) requires employers to set up a system to receive and appropriately respond to consultations, to take measures needed to deter customer conduct so that the response is effective, and to take other necessary employment management measures. Article 33(2) prohibits dismissal or other disadvantageous treatment of a worker who consulted or gave facts during the employer's response. Article 33(4) directs the Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare to issue a guideline.

That guideline is the "Guidelines on Measures Employers Should Take in Employment Management Regarding Problems Arising from the Conduct of Customers and Others in the Workplace" (事業主が職場における顧客等の言動に起因する問題に関して雇用管理上講ずべき措置等についての指針, MHLW Notice No. 51 of 2026). The [Yamanashi Labor Bureau](https://jsite.mhlw.go.jp/yamanashi-roudoukyoku/hourei_seido_tetsuzuki/houkaisei_goannai/newpage_00004.html) records that it and the job seeker sexual harassment guideline were promulgated on February 26, 2026. As at November 2026, no English translation has been published, so this page works from the Japanese text.

blocks.title: Relationship to power harassment duties
blocks.text: The customer harassment measures sit beside the existing [power harassment prevention duty](/regulations/japan-power-harassment-prevention-obligations), which Act No. 63 of 2025 renumbered from Article 30-2 to Article 31. The Guideline allows one consultation desk to handle both. The content differs because the person causing harm is outside the employer's control.

sections.heading: What counts as customer harassment under the Guideline?

blocks.text: Workplace customer harassment is conduct that meets all three elements: (1) conduct by customers or others connected with the business, (2) that exceeds what is socially acceptable in light of the nature of the worker's duties and other circumstances, and (3) that harms the worker's working environment. The [Guideline](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11900000/001662584.pdf) states that not every complaint is harassment: a complaint made within socially acceptable limits is a legitimate request.

items: **Customers and others** include potential customers, prospective business partners, staff of business partners, people negotiating contracts, users of facilities such as stations, airports, hospitals, schools, welfare and public facilities and their families, and neighbors of a facility.
**The workplace** is anywhere the worker performs their duties, including a business partner's office, a restaurant used for a meeting, or a customer's home.
**The channel does not matter.** Conduct by telephone and on social media and other online platforms is included, not only face to face conduct in stores and facilities.

**Requests by persons with disabilities** not to be discriminated against, or for removal of social barriers, are not customer harassment. Employers must still provide reasonable accommodation under the Act on the Elimination of Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities where the burden is not excessive.
**Single incidents can qualify.** Frequency and persistence are considered, but conduct causing strong physical or mental distress can harm the working environment on one occasion.

blocks.text: Whether conduct crosses the line is judged on all the circumstances, including its purpose, the background and any problem behavior by the worker, the industry, the frequency of the conduct, and the worker's attributes. The Guideline adds that an inappropriate response by the employer or worker can be the cause of the conduct, so training should cover service quality as well as how to respond.

Employers must take ten measures in five groups. The MHLW [detailed leaflet](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11900000/001662580.pdf) numbers them as follows and marks measures 1, 2 and 8 as specific to customer harassment.

items: **Policy.** Clarify a policy that the employer will respond firmly to customer harassment and protect workers, and communicate it to all workers including managers and supervisors.
**Predefined response procedures.** Decide in advance how workers and managers will respond, and communicate both what customer harassment is and those procedures to workers.
**Consultation desk.** Designate a desk in advance and make it known. It can be combined with the desk for other forms of harassment.
**Desk capability.** Ensure desk staff can respond appropriately, including to borderline cases and cases where harassment may occur.
**Confirm the facts.** Establish the facts promptly and accurately, which can include asking the perpetrator's employer to cooperate where the perpetrator works for another business.
**Care for the affected worker.** Where harassment is confirmed, promptly take measures for the affected worker.
**Prevent recurrence.** Communicate the policy again and fix underlying problems in products, services or customer handling. This applies even when the facts could not be confirmed.

**Especially malicious conduct.** Decide in advance how to deal with especially malicious conduct, such as repeated excessive demands, make it known to workers, and set up the internal coordination needed to act on it.
**Privacy.** Protect the privacy of those involved, including sensitive information such as sexual orientation and gender identity, and tell workers this is done.

**No retaliation.** State that workers will not be dismissed or treated disadvantageously for consulting, cooperating, or using the Prefectural Labor Bureau's assistance or mediation, and make this known.

blocks.text: The Guideline gives examples of predefined responses, stressing that the list is not exhaustive: report to a manager immediately and take instructions; avoid leaving a worker to respond alone and let a manager take over if needed; record interactions in compliance with the Act on the Protection of Personal Information; end the visit or call after a reasonable time if demands continue after a full explanation; report possible crimes such as assault, injury or threats to the police; escalate to head office; and consult lawyers through the legal department.

For especially malicious conduct, the examples are reporting to the police, sending a warning letter, refusing to sell or provide services within the limits of the law, banning the person from stores and facilities, and applying for a provisional disposition under the Civil Provisional Remedies Act. The Guideline also reminds employers to respect consumer rights, disability discrimination law, and sector laws that oblige continued service, for example where interrupting a service would seriously affect someone's life or health.

Training is not a stand-alone legal requirement, but the Guideline names it as an accepted way to meet five of the measures, and Article 34(2) creates a separate training effort duty. Employers must communicate the policy and the response procedures by some effective means, and the Guideline lists training and lectures (kenshū, kōshū tō) as an example for both, alongside internal newsletters, intranet pages and response manuals.

items: **Policy and procedures.** Training that explains the firm response policy together with the predefined procedures, and training that explains what customer harassment is and how to respond.
**Consultation desk staff.** Training on how to respond when a consultation is received, and training on privacy protection.
**Recurrence prevention.** Delivering training on the policy and procedures again after a case.

**Desirable measures.** Training on customer service, the employer's products and services, and complaint handling, so workers can understand what they sell and respond well; and training on consumer psychology and disability characteristics.

blocks.text: Article 34(2) requires employers to endeavor to deepen workers' understanding of customer harassment problems and to ensure workers pay necessary attention to their own conduct toward other employers' workers, "through the implementation of training and other necessary consideration" (研修の実施その他の必要な配慮). This covers the employer's own staff when they act as customers or business partners. Article 34(3) asks employers themselves, and for a company its officers, to endeavor to deepen their own understanding.

sections.heading: What about your own staff's conduct toward other companies' workers?

blocks.text: The rules cut both ways: an employer must try to cooperate when another employer investigates its staff, and must try to stop its own staff harassing other employers' workers. Article 33(3) requires employers to endeavor to comply when another employer asks for cooperation with its measures, such as fact finding. The Guideline says terminating a contract because cooperation was requested is undesirable, and that it is desirable to protect workers who cooperate and to discipline staff found to have harassed.

Article 34(5) also places an effort duty on customers themselves to pay attention so that their conduct does not harm workers' working environment. The Guideline describes it as desirable for the employer's policy to state that its own workers must not engage in customer harassment toward other employers' workers, and to extend the protective policy to people working on its premises who are not its employees, such as a manufacturer's staff selling in a retail store.

On the same date, measures against sexual harassment of job seekers became mandatory under Article 13 of the [Equal Employment Opportunity Act](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347AC0000000113/20261001_507AC0000000063), with a training effort duty in Article 14(2). The [job seeker Guideline](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/11900000/001662589.pdf) (MHLW Notice No. 52 of 2026) covers applicants, participants in recruiting activities, and trainees on teaching, nursing and other placements, including activity online.

Most measures mirror the customer harassment measures, but one is new: employers must set rules for job seeking activities in advance, such as the time and place of interviews, who attends, and which social media can be used for contact, and make them known to both workers and job seekers. Recruiters, interviewers and internship supervisors therefore need their own training content.

sections.heading: What happens if an employer does not comply?

blocks.text: As at November 2026, there is no fine or criminal penalty for failing to take the measures. Under Article 42, the Minister, acting through the Prefectural Labor Bureaus, may give advice, guidance or recommendations, and may publish the name of an employer that violates Article 33(1) or (2) and does not follow a recommendation. Under Article 45 the Minister can require reports, and failing to report or reporting falsely is subject to a non-criminal fine (karyō) of up to 200,000 yen under Article 51.

Workers can ask the Director of the Prefectural Labor Bureau for dispute resolution assistance under Article 36 or request mediation under Article 37, and employers must not retaliate for either. The Guideline also lists mediation as a route when the facts cannot be confirmed. Civil liability to a harmed worker is a separate risk, so the records below matter in litigation as well.

sections.heading: How do you evidence customer harassment prevention?

blocks.text: Keep a dated record for each of the ten measures, with version history. A practical checklist follows.

items: The firm response policy, the top message announcing it, and any public notice to customers.
The predefined response procedures for each site type and channel (store, phone, online), and the customer response manual that contains them.
Records of how both were communicated: training completion by role, intranet posts, distributed materials.
The consultation desk designation, how workers were told about it, and desk staff training on response and privacy.
The especially malicious conduct policy and the internal coordination procedure behind it.
Work rules or similar documents stating that workers will not be disadvantaged for consulting or cooperating.
Case files showing fact finding, measures for the worker, and recurrence prevention, stored with restricted access.
Evidence that the policy, procedures and training are reviewed, for example through worker surveys or the health committee, which the Guideline mentions as a desirable route.

blocks.text: For change control across sites, see [updating training when a regulation changes](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change). Multinational groups can compare these duties with [Australia's psychosocial hazard requirements](/regulations/psychosocial-hazards-training-requirements), which also cover harm from customers and clients.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each of the ten Guideline measures and the Article 34 effort duty as obligations, links them to the employer's policy, response manual and work rules, and defines role based learning outcomes and assessment points for customer facing workers, managers and desk staff. The power harassment and customer harassment obligations share a consultation desk node, so a change to either shows which modules and assessments need review.

faqs.q: Does the customer harassment duty apply to small businesses in Japan?
faqs.a: Yes. Article 33 applies to all employers from October 1, 2026, with no headcount threshold and no transitional effort duty period for small and medium enterprises. Unlike the power harassment duty, which was phased in for SMEs, the customer harassment measures took effect for every employer on the same date.

faqs.q: Is every customer complaint customer harassment?
faqs.a: No. The Guideline states that complaints made within socially acceptable limits are legitimate requests, and that workers should handle them sincerely. Conduct becomes customer harassment only when its content or its means exceeds what is socially acceptable and it harms the worker's working environment. Either the content or the means alone can be enough.

faqs.q: Can a business refuse service to a customer who harasses staff?
faqs.a: The Guideline lists refusing to sell goods or provide services, within the limits of the law, as an example response to especially malicious conduct, along with warnings, entry bans and police reports. Employers must take sector laws into account, for example where a service must legally be provided or interruption would seriously affect someone's life or health.

faqs.q: How often should customer harassment training be delivered?
faqs.a: Neither the Act nor the Guideline sets a frequency. The Guideline requires the policy and procedures to be made known and lists renewed training as a recurrence prevention step after a case. A reasonable pattern is training at hiring, on promotion to a supervisory role, and when the procedures change.

faqs.q: Can recording customers be part of the response procedures?
faqs.a: Yes. Recording or filming interactions is one of the Guideline's example responses, and recordings can be used to confirm facts. The Guideline requires employers to comply with the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and handle customers' personal information appropriately when they record and when they review recordings.
